content.title: A knob far from the loss
content.text: The random start again, reading the 7: the score for 7 is 11.59%, the loss 2.1554. Pick the knob of pill 05, pixel 21 into neuron 10 of the first row, at 0.156. Between it and the loss sit neuron 10’s squash, 16 neurons of the second row, 10 scores and the loss itself: 160 paths. Nudging this knob and measuring the 7’s loss again gives its slope, −0.03421, at the price of a whole extra pass. The question of this pill: the same number from the slopes of the single steps, with no nudge at all.

content.title: Slopes multiply along a path
content.text: Start at the knob. Its first step is the sum: z of neuron 10 moves 0.625 per unit of the knob, the input on the wire, as pill 08 showed. The second step is the squash: at z = 0.509 the S-curve has slope 0.7798. Nudge the knob by a hair, d. Then z moves 0.625 d, and the squash output moves 0.7798 × 0.625 d = 0.4874 d. Slopes multiply, like gears: if the first turns the second at 0.625 per turn and the second turns the third at 0.7798, the first turns the third at their product. That is the chain rule, all of it. Each step needs to know only its own slope.

content.title: The last two steps
content.text: Now the far end, where every path arrives. The final step, score 7 into the loss, has a slope that the maths of −log and softmax makes simple: the score minus its target. For the right digit, 0.1159 − 1 = −0.8841; for a wrong digit it is the score itself. One step before it, knob A of pill 08 feeds score 7 from hidden neuron 6, whose output is 0.1402: that input is the slope. Multiply: 0.1402 × (−0.8841) = −0.1240, the slope of this picture’s loss against knob A. Nudging says −0.1240. Two local slopes, one multiplication, no nudge.

content.title: Paths add
content.text: A hidden neuron is not on one path. Neuron 14 of the second row feeds all 10 scores, so a nudge to its output reaches the loss ten ways at once. Along each path, multiply: the wire’s weight times that score’s slope. Ten products, most of them small, one large through score 7: −0.7154 × (−0.8841) = 0.6325. Across paths, add: 0.6702, the slope of the loss against neuron 14’s output. Back through its own squash, × 0.9544, gives 0.6396, its blame. One knob into it, from neuron 25 of the first row with input −0.9219: slope −0.5896, and nudging agrees. Multiply along a path, add across paths.

content.title: Walk back once
content.text: Look at the pattern: a neuron’s slope comes only from the row after it. So start at the loss and walk back one row at a time. The 10 scores first: score minus target. Then the 16: add across the 10 paths, times the squash. Then the 32, the same way. Every neuron ends up with one number, its blame. Every knob’s slope is then its neuron’s blame times its input. Pixel 21 into neuron 10: −0.05474 × 0.625 = −0.03421, the number nudging gave in the first step. One backward walk, all 2,778 slopes. Averaged over the 3,823 pictures, it is the field of pill 08.

content.title: Why this is the whole trick
content.text: Count the work. One forward pass gives every value in the network; one backward walk, about the same size, gives every slope. Two passes for 2,778 slopes, where nudging needed 2,779. And the walk does not care how many knobs there are: 2,778 or two billion, one pass each way. This is the trick that let networks grow, and the last piece of the recipe: a network, a loss, and a slope for every knob. Pill 10 runs the whole of it on one neuron with every number visible; pill 11 trains the digit network with it on screen.
